### Problem: Two city scheduling {#sec-pf-p3-two-city}

::: {.p-statement}
$2n$ people ($1 \le n \le 50$) must be flown to two cities, exactly $n$ to each. Person $i$ costs $a_i$ to fly to city A and $b_i$ to city B. Minimise the total cost.

Source: [LC 1029 · Two City Scheduling](https://leetcode.com/problems/two-city-scheduling/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Start by sending everyone to B, costing $\sum b_i$. Switching person $i$ to A changes the cost by $a_i - b_i$. We must switch exactly $n$ people, so switch the $n$ with the smallest $a_i - b_i$.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
Sort by $d_i = a_i - b_i$; send the first $n$ to A and the rest to B.

**Exchange proof.** Suppose an optimal assignment sends $i$ to B and $j$ to A with $d_i < d_j$. Swapping them (i to A, j to B) keeps $n$ per city and changes the cost by $(a_i - b_i) - (a_j - b_j) = d_i - d_j < 0$: strictly better, contradicting optimality (or equal when $d_i = d_j$). So in an optimal assignment everyone in A has $d \le$ everyone in B, which is exactly the sorted split.

The reformulation $\text{cost} = \sum_i b_i + \sum_{i \in A} d_i$ also proves it directly: we minimise a sum of exactly $n$ of the $d_i$.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
#### Python

```{python}
#| label: pf-two-city
def two_city(costs):
    costs = sorted(costs, key=lambda c: c[0] - c[1])
    n = len(costs) // 2
    return sum(a for a, _ in costs[:n]) + sum(b for _, b in costs[n:])

def two_city_brute(costs):
    m = len(costs)
    return min(sum(costs[i][0] if i in A else costs[i][1] for i in range(m))
               for A in map(set, combinations(range(m), m // 2)))

for _ in range(500):
    n = random.randint(1, 5)
    costs = [(random.randint(1, 50), random.randint(1, 50)) for _ in range(2 * n)]
    assert two_city(costs) == two_city_brute(costs)

assert two_city([(10, 20), (30, 200), (400, 50), (30, 20)]) == 110
assert two_city([(259, 770), (448, 54), (926, 667), (184, 139), (840, 118), (577, 469)]) == 1859
```

#### C++

```cpp
int twoCitySchedCost(vector<vector<int>>& c) {
    sort(c.begin(), c.end(), [](auto& x, auto& y) { return x[0] - x[1] < y[0] - y[1]; });
    int n = c.size() / 2, total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 2 * n; ++i) total += (i < n) ? c[i][0] : c[i][1];
    return total;
}
```
:::

::: {#fig-pf-two-city}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
costs = [(259, 770), (448, 54), (926, 667), (184, 139), (840, 118), (577, 469)]
order = sorted(costs, key=lambda c: c[0] - c[1])
assert two_city(costs) == 1859
def city(ax, p):
    d = [a_ - b_ for a_, b_ in order]
    colors = [p["soft"]["indigo"]] * 3 + [p["soft"]["amber"]] * 3
    edges = [p["indigo"]] * 3 + [p["amber"]] * 3
    ax.bar(range(6), d, color=colors, edgecolor=edges)
    ax.axhline(0, color=p["line"], lw=1)
    ax.set_xticks(range(6), [f"({a_},{b_})" for a_, b_ in order], fontsize=8)
    ax.set_ylabel("a − b")
    ax.text(1, max(d) * 0.9, "to city A", color=p["indigo"], ha="center")
    ax.text(3.2, max(d) * 0.9, "to city B", color=p["amber"], ha="center")
V.plot(city, size=(6.4, 3.0))
```

The six people of the second sample sorted by a − b. The three with the smallest a − b (most money saved by flying to A) go to A; the rest go to B. Total 1859.

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Time** $O(n\log n)$. **Space** $O(1)$ beyond the sort.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- Ties in $a_i - b_i$: any order among tied people gives the same cost.
- Sorting by $a_i$ alone, or by $\min(a_i, b_i)$, is wrong; the brute force catches it at once.
:::
